inline.s: What makes love love lies in its weight and lightness, its thickness and thinness; it has its proper reward and its dependent reward. To enumerate its kinds: father, mother, wife, and child; brothers and friends; fame, rank, wealth, and honor; essays, poems, and verse; arts and techniques; clothes, food, and drink; houses, fields, and gardens; woods, springs, flowers, and landscape; treasures and playthings, all manner of fine and delightful things, too many to list one by one. Among them there is what is great, heavier than Mount Tai, and what is small, lighter than a swan's down. To have one thing one cannot forget is love; to have one thought one cannot let go is love. If even a single love lingers in the breast, the one-thought recitation of the Buddha's name is not unified; if a single thought does not return to unity, one cannot be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Kun di (kun di): brothers.

Alas! "If love is not heavy, one is not born in Saha; if the thought is not one, one is not reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss." These two lines may be called the golden blade that scrapes away the film over a clouded eye, and the holy medicine that cures the heart's fatal disease. All who are resolved to seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss should write these words upon the walls of their dwellings and engrave them upon their very flesh, reciting them solemnly at every moment and calling them to mind with every thought. Toward the loves of Saha, seek every day to make them lighter; toward the thought of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, seek every day to make it one. Lighter and lighter, until by degrees one reaches the state of having none; one and one again, until by degrees one draws near the utmost. If one can truly do this, then though this person has not yet escaped Saha, he is no longer a long dweller in Saha; though he has not yet been reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, he is already an honored guest of that land. When the right thought appears before death, rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss is certain.

Alas! These two lines, "If love is not heavy, one is not born in Saha; if the thought is not one, one is not reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss," may well be called the golden blade that scrapes the film from a clouded eye and the holy medicine that cures the heart's fatal disease. All who are resolved to seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss should write these two lines upon the wall, engrave them upon their flesh, recite them solemnly at every moment, and call them to mind with every thought. Toward the loves of Saha, seek every day to make them lighter; toward the thought of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, seek every day to make it one. Love, lighter and lighter, until by degrees it reaches the state of having none; thought, one and one again, until by degrees it reaches the utmost. If one can truly do this, then though this person has not yet left Saha, he is no longer a long dweller in Saha; though he has not yet been reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, he is already an honored guest of that land. When the right thought appears before death, rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss is certain.

Gua yi yan zhi jin bi (the golden blade that scrapes the film from a clouded eye): jin bi, i.e., jin bi, pronounced pi and bi. This was a medical implement of ancient times, used to scrape away the film that covers the surface of the eyeball, thereby restoring sight. Gao huang (the vital regions): refers to a fatal disease.

Someone asked, "Is there a method for lightness of love?" The answer: "Nothing is more essential for lightness of love than unifying the thought." Again he asked, "Is there a method for unifying the thought?" The answer: "Nothing is more essential for unifying the thought than lightness of love." The man smiled and said, "Master, your words waver between two ends, seeming to hold no single standard, and so leave the student nothing to follow." The answer: "It is not two ends; I wish to make clear the reason why the thought must be unified. For the thought (of reciting the Buddha's name) cannot be single-minded because the scattered mind clings to other objects; and the scattered mind's clinging to other objects is in turn caused by chasing the realm and rushing about in confusion. Therefore, when there is one realm in Saha, the beings have one mind; when beings have one mind, there is one realm in Saha. Hence it is said, "When the mind arises, various dharmas arise; when dharmas arise, various minds arise." Gathering conditions, the mind stirs within; rushing outward, it dashes about. Mind and realm chase each other, and not even the dusts of a kalpa could exhaust them. If love is not forgotten, can the thought ever be unified?"

Someone asked, "Is there a method for lightness of love?" The answer: "The key to lightness of love is to unify the thought." Again he asked, "Is there a method for unifying the thought?" The answer: "The key to unifying the thought is lightness of love." The man smiled and said, "Master, your words waver without a fixed view, leaving the student with nothing to follow." The answer: "It is not wavering; this is to make clear the reason why the thought must be unified. For the thought (of reciting the Buddha's name) cannot be single-minded because the mind, scattered, clings to other objects. And the mind's scattered clinging to other objects is in turn caused by chasing the realm and rushing about. Therefore, when there is one realm in Saha, the beings have one mind; when beings have one mind, there is one realm in Saha. Hence it is said, "When the mind arises, various dharmas arise; when dharmas arise, various minds arise." When conditions gather, the mind arises; chasing the realm, the mind dashes off. The mind conditions the realm and the realm pulls the mind; mind and realm race together, and not even the dusts of a kalpa could exhaust them. If love is not broken, can the thought ever be single-minded?"
Ai gou bu wang (if love is not forgotten): if love is not extinguished. In classical writing "wang" is used for "wang," meaning "to extinguish."

Wan er (to smile): the look of a gentle smile. Shou shu liang duan (the rat hesitating at both ends): wavering between the two. "Shou shu": the rat is by nature suspicious and, when emerging from its hole, thrusts out its head now and draws it back now. "Liang duan": whether to advance or retreat, unable to make up its mind.

Thus, to unify the thought, nothing surpasses lightening the love; to lighten the love, nothing surpasses unifying the mind. To unify the mind, nothing surpasses shutting off the realm. When all realms are empty, all conditions fall still; when all conditions fall still, the single thought accomplishes itself. Should the single thought be accomplished, the conditions of love are all exhausted. Hence it is said: "To unify the thought, nothing surpasses lightening the love; to lighten the love, nothing surpasses the single thought." For love and the one-thought cannot stand together, like the alternation of sun and moon, or the turning-away of bright and dark.]

Thus, to unify the thought, nothing surpasses lightening the love; to lighten the love, nothing surpasses unifying the mind. To unify the mind, nothing surpasses shutting off the realm (letting the mind not clothe the realm); when all realms are empty, all conditions fall still; when all conditions fall still, the single thought accomplishes itself (the pure one-thought of Buddha-recitation is naturally accomplished). Should the single thought be accomplished, the conditions of love are all exhausted. Hence it is said: "To unify the thought, nothing surpasses lightening the love; to lighten the love, nothing surpasses the single thought." For the conditions of love and the one-thought cannot stand together, like the alternation of night and day, or the utter opposition of dark and light. (Thus the severing of love and the unifying of the thought reinforce each other.)
Question: To let go of all conditions and with single mind recite the Buddha seeking rebirth in the Pure Land, is this not merely seeking one's own benefit?
Answer: Master Yinguang said:

"One cannot yet save oneself, yet wishes to save others: how is this different from drowning in the sea and trying to rescue a man? I urge you good sages: do not be proud and lofty toward yourselves; better to hold true faith and firm vows and, relying on the compassionate power, recite the Buddha and seek rebirth in the West."
(From a discourse on Buddha-recitation at the Shanghai Fazang Monastery.)
Zi jing (self-admonishment): self-warning. In these seven self-admonishments, Master Zhuhong explicitly specifies which things must not be done, in order to maintain a single-minded right thought.
Master Zhuhong, in the Posthumous Writings of Master Yunqi
Self-Admonishments, says:

The ancients had a saying: "Yu, a sage, begrudged even a single inch of the sun's light; as for us, we should begrudge even a single minute." I am now old and worn; it is more than a mere minute I should begrudge, but even in the space of a snap of the fingers I must not mix my mind with other thoughts.

The ancients said: "Da Yu was a sage and still begrudged a single inch of time; we, then, should begrudge a single minute." I am now aged and frail; do I merely begrudge a single minute? Even in the space of a snap of the fingers, I must not use my mind in a confused way!

Xian min you yan (the ancients had a saying): Tao Kan, the famed general of the Jin dynasty, used to say to others, "Da Yu was a sage and begrudged even an inch of the sun's light; we should begrudge even a minute." Cun yin (an inch of light): very brief time, from the Huainanzi, "Discourse on the Original Way": "The sage does not value the best of a foot-long jade, but values the inch of the sun's light, because time is hard to obtain and easy to lose." Guang yin (time): duration. Chi zhi bi (a foot-long jade): a jade disc a foot in diameter. Bi yu (jade): a superior fine jade. Xi chi (xi chi, meaning "what need to mention"): how much more; not merely.

Wua za yong xin zhe (as to not mixing the mind with other thoughts): it says that apart from the right thought of one's own practice, the moment a single stray thought arises one should sweep it away and gather it back to the right thought, without the least delay. I will now briefly open up seven matters; those who truly leave the household life because of birth and death, who wish to settle the great matter in this very life, must strive to keep them and warn themselves at every moment.

Not to mix the mind with other thoughts means this: apart from the right thought of one's own practice, the moment a single stray thought arises one must sweep it away at once and gather it back to the right thought, without a moment's delay. I now briefly raise seven matters. Those who truly leave the household life because of birth and death and wish to settle the great affair in this very life should strive with all their might to keep them, warning themselves at every moment.

Ben can zheng nian (the primary right thought): Master Zhuhong cultivated the samadhi of Buddha-recitation through the method of investigation (canjiu), so his primary right thought is "Amitabha Buddha." Master Zhuhong said:

"Taking up the huatou is the most urgent work for awakening in the Chan school. One who cultivates the Pure Land may take the single phrase of the Buddha's name as a huatou; this is a marvellous method."
Again he said:
"Now, when idle thoughts clamour and fly about, simply lift lightly the Buddha
(the Buddha's name)
a single phrase and it settles; watch then who it is that recites the Buddha's name. If after a long while thoughts arise
(if stray thoughts arise)
, lift again in this way and watch in this way; if no thought arises, just keep watching."
(From the Collected Sayings on the Pure Land of Yunqi.) As to investigating the Buddha's name and the samadhi of Buddha-recitation, see in detail
The Treatise on the Samadhi of Buddha-Recitation

One: do not hoard wealth, build houses, buy fields, or provide yourself with any fine and lovely thing. Even sutras and images handed down from antiquity, even works by famous masters, do not cling to; keep a single-minded right thought.

One: do not hoard up wealth, build houses, buy land, or procure all manner of exquisite goods. Even sutra images handed down from antiquity, even works from famous hands, are not to be cherished; keep a single-minded right thought.

Yi xin zheng nian (a single-minded right thought): Master Zhuhong said: "One resolute in study has but a single right thought dwelling constantly in his breast. In stillness it is thus, in disturbance it is thus; let stillness and disturbance change as they will, this thought of mine is never shifted in the least; only thus is there no interruption, and this is called doing one's work well. Have you not seen the ancients say: the wise clear the mind, the foolish clear the realm? If one must shun the noisy and take the still, then I fear there is no time of stillness in the realm, and no place of stillness. He who seeks stillness had best dwell in the deep mountains. But the mountains are still, yet the woodcutter's axe is heard beyond the clouds and the shepherd's flute sounds in the setting sun, so how can the ear be still? And though the axe and the flute might be shut away so they reach not the ear, as for apes crying and tigers roaring in the clear night, and magpies chattering and crows crying in the bright day, how can the realm be still? Yet the ape's cry and tiger's roar, the magpie's chatter and crow's caw, might be driven off so they reach not the ear; but when the wild wind rises and a thousand hollows howl, when swift thunder breaks and a thousand mountains shake, will the one who shuns the noisy for the silent shut them away, or drive them off? From this we see that the realm surely has no time of stillness, and surely no place of stillness. A student is only to be pitied if his resolve is not fierce! Hold a fierce resolve, and where can he not go?" (From the Collected Writings of Yunqi.)

Two: do not do all manner of meritorious-condition affairs that are not urgent; leave them until the great affair is made clear, for it is not too late then. For now set aside the gate of manifold practices, keeping a single-minded right thought.

Two: do not do all manner of meritorious-condition affairs that are not urgent; leave them until the great affair is made clear, and then it is not too late. For the present, set aside the gate of manifold practices, keeping a single-minded right thought.

Da shi (the great affair): here it refers to seeing one's nature and clarifying the mind. For a practitioner of Buddha-recitation who has not yet attained single-mindedness, single-minded unsullied recitation is the foremost great affair of escaping birth and death. Wan xing men (the gate of manifold practices): "wan xing" means all the methods of practice; "men" (gate) carries the sense of entering and departing. The Chan master Guishan Lingyou said: "In the ground of reality not a single mote is received; in the gate of manifold practices not a single dharma is forsaken." (From the Record of Chan Master Guishan Lingyou of Tanzhou.)

Three: do not, toward pleasant forms and pleasant tastes and the like, give rise to a greedy and clinging mind; toward those who praise me with pleasing words, give rise to a greedy and clinging mind. Do not, toward disagreeable forms and tastes and the like, give rise to an angry and vexed mind; toward those who slander me with harsh words, who scold and insult me, who in every manner thwart me, give rise to an angry and vexed mind. Even concerning the past and the future, whether agreeable or contrary, shut them all away, hold the wall firm and keep stanch, keeping a single-minded right thought.

Three: do not, toward pleasant forms and sweet tastes and the like, give rise to a greedy and clinging mind; toward those who praise me with pleasing words, give rise to a greedy and clinging mind. Do not, toward disagreeable forms and foul tastes and the like, give rise to an angry and vexed mind; toward those who slander me with harsh words, who scold and insult me, who in every manner thwart me, give rise to an angry and vexed mind. Even the affairs of past and future, whether agreeable or contrary, are all to be shut off and cut away
shut off and cut away
, without giving rise to a mind of love or hate, of taking or rejecting; hold the wall firm and keep stanch, keeping a single-minded right thought.
Jian bi (the firm wall): a firm and sturdy rampart.

Four: do not chant or compose poetry and prose, write out in regular or running script the inscriptions and couplets, embellish the letters you send, or browse through non-Buddhist books. Do not discuss the right and wrong, the strengths and weaknesses, of others; even less, relying on one's private opinions, should you compose works with a self-inflated mind; and if your Chan has not yet pierced through, do not recklessly take up old gongans to criticize and appraise; rather keep the mouth sealed and the tongue tied, keeping a single-minded right thought.

Four: do not chant or compose poetry and prose, write out in regular (true) or running script the inscriptions and couplets, or polish the letters (chi du) you send, or browse through non-Buddhist books. Do not discuss the right and wrong, the strengths and weaknesses, of others; even less, relying on one's own private view, should you, with an inflated mind, compose writings. If your Chan has not yet pierced through, do not recklessly take up the old gongans to comment and appraise; rather keep the mouth sealed and the tongue tied, keeping a single-minded right thought.

Xiu shi chi du (to polish the letters): revising and polishing the wording of one's letters to make them beautiful. Wai shu (non-Buddhist books): the Buddhist canon is the inner canon; everything outside it is called the outer canon. Yi jian (private view): one's own private opinion. Nian ping (to take up and appraise): taking up old gongans to point them out and comment upon them; "nian gu" is to pick out an old gongan case to awaken a Chan practitioner, and "ping chang" is to appraise and promote the sayings of the ancients.
